2026-10-01 (Codex, Lotka-Volterra and offline simulator discussion; proposal only): user proposes running interchangeable ecological models and the existing state machine on a geological map outside Minecraft, measuring density, encounters and death ratios. Recommended: build a reproducible spatial experiment before choosing new production defaults. Classic Lotka-Volterra models aggregate prey growth, predation and predator losses. It has no locations, obstacles, sensory conditions or player encounters, assumes continuous populations and can miss extinction in small discrete populations. Its ideal population cycles do not establish good gameplay. Retain it as a reference model or a calibrated coarse population layer, not as a replacement for individual decision states. Habitat carrying capacity, finite food regeneration, bounded consumption, integer groups, explicit recruitment/reproduction, mortality and migration are candidates for the spatial model. The current mind changes needs and consumes meals but does not itself implement population reproduction or starvation deaths; these would be deliberate new rules. Separate ecological capacity from performance caps and pacing targets.
Architecture: reuse the real Java WildlifeMind, DailySchedule, tier classification and applicable ambient/choreography timing in a standalone runner. WildlifeMind is already deterministic and independent of world access. Supply terrain, sensing, movement, spawn and combat observations through adapters shared with or calibrated against the mod. Reusing the mind alone is insufficient: WildlifeGoal and the Minecraft engine currently decide which stimuli and paths are possible. The showcase recorder injects hypothetical scenes, so its transition matrices are not an encounter simulator. Provide modes for the faithful current baseline, geometry/density corrections only, spatial resource/prey/predator ecology with the same state machine, and an aggregate LV reference whose encounter metrics are explicitly unavailable. Keep encounter scheduling, camp stimuli, day-carnivore policy, group placement and population density separately switchable so a combined change does not hide its cause. Show a map, state/route overlays, time-series plots, seed and parameter controls, replay and event logs. Reset to the same saved initial state for model comparisons; arbitrary live switching must not create or delete populations implicitly.
Terrain: the proposed geological map should include elevation, habitat and danger bands, water and accessible banks, forage and regrowth, shelter, slope, canopy, obstacles, species-sized body clearance and connectivity, plus base walls/gates and surface stimulus locations. A chunk-level average or simple heightmap cannot represent a Rex blocked by trees, a narrow pass, an overhang or a cave entrance. Use finer navigation/occlusion information near obstacles, model underground space separately when needed, and track dynamic construction/terrain changes. Start with synthetic open plains, forest, river, cliff and enclosed-base fixtures, then import snapshots exported from real generated worlds. For example, a 64 by 64 chunk region with a central measurement area and an outer buffer is a starting experiment size, not a performance claim. Record edge immigration/emigration explicitly; avoid artificial wraparound routes and test sensitivity to region size and buffer width.
Experiments and validation: repeat scripted three-hour crafting, shallow/deep mining with surfacing, slow/fast Creative flight, walking, hunting, cleared-local-wildlife and overlapping-player scenarios across terrain seeds, weather, time of day, base designs and parameter sets. Use the same maps and scenario schedules, paired random seeds with separate random streams for subsystems, consistent initial populations and simulated time units. Separate warm-up from observations and add longer runs to reveal delayed population collapse or boom. Report distributions and uncertainty, including runs with zero encounters, not one attractive replay or only averages. Tune on one set of maps/seeds and validate on held-out ones. Check population conservation and numerical/time-step sensitivity and compare baseline adapter traces with actual runtime traces. Use the fast offline runner for parameter searches, the real NeoForge headless server for placement/navigation/collision/combat and tier transitions, then client playtests for visibility, sound readability and fairness. Calibrate against several observed patterns; matching only total population is not predictive validation. Offline execution time does not predict Minecraft server tick cost, which must be profiled in the real engine.
Metrics: count individuals and distinct groups by species, habitat and distance ring, density over usable habitat, occupancy, travel and failed paths, ecological extinction/recovery, births/recruitment, immigration/emigration, kills and natural mortality. Define mortality as deaths per animal-hour and report causes, keeping budget culls/despawns separate from biological deaths; preserve separate player deaths per player-hour or encounter and tame losses. Distinguish a group passing the base, wildlife visible/audible to the player, investigation of surface camp stimuli, actual player detection/threat and attacks/damage. De-duplicate repeat ticks by group/episode. Record encounter gaps (including zero-encounter runs), time to first visible wildlife while travelling, species diversity and local spawn/delete churn. While the player mines underground, a surface visitor is a base visit, not a witnessed encounter; measure events after surfacing separately. Track nearest-radius density as well as whole-region totals, and real server tick-time/memory cost. Good ecological coexistence can still produce an empty-feeling or exhausting game.
Runtime option if validated: keep cheap region/group records outside the entity simulation and instantiate real creatures only on valid loaded terrain. Advance distant ecological state with bounded slower updates, preserve needs/identity across representation changes and ensure exactly one system owns each birth, death and migration. Never apply aggregate predation losses to the same loaded animals whose combat is already being simulated. Actual kills and player actions feed the regional ledger. Preserve tames and other protected entities, persistence through saves, overlap-aware multiplayer accounting and strict physical spawn limits. Use cached/exported terrain or conservative unknown-terrain handling without forcing live chunk loads or inventing paths through ungenerated terrain. This abstract offscreen ecology would be a new feature, not something the current model already does. A closed ecosystem can empty regions after hunting; any recolonization, population floor or immigration must be explicit and measured, since constant refilling can conceal ecological failure. Ecology and encounter scheduling remain independent so the experiment can determine whether scheduling is needed.
Reply to the latest Opus proposal: include his near-ring group quotas, forward placement, real surface camp scent/work noise, bounded investigation and daytime-carnivore filter changes as experiments. Agree that pass-bys alone do not prove interaction, but do not optimize only player focus: visible wildlife and noncombat base visits are also useful outcomes. Prefer readable stimuli from actual surface activities to unavoidable attraction based solely on time at home. Measure base visits, investigation and aggression separately, and do not accumulate an attack backlog while the player is unreachable underground. Prior numeric density and pacing targets from either author remain hypotheses until these comparisons. Recommendation: prototype a faithful baseline plus one spatial ecology variant before a whole-world system; the useful goal is statistical prediction and ranking designs, not an exact future encounter timeline. No simulator, LV runtime or gameplay change has been implemented in this task.

2026-10-01 (Claude Opus 5.5, Lotka-Volterra and simulator discussion; not implemented): measured, not argued. A stochastic literal Lotka-Volterra at this scale (20 prey and 4 predators per region, 10-day cycle, 1000 regions, 100 in-game days) lost its predators in every region (median day 8) and its prey passed 5000 in 79 percent. The same equilibrium as a stochastic Rosenzweig-MacArthur model (logistic prey, saturating predation) with a small immigration floor holds, but noise dominates: no predator in a region 20 percent of the time, predators 0 to 10 (5 to 95 percent). On continuous regional densities, without individual noise, it can be tuned: below its threshold it settles; just above (carrying capacity 105 against a threshold of 100) it cycles prey 9 to 38 and predators 1 to 9 every 7 in-game days and returns to the same cycle after the predators are halved, but only after weeks; checked with RK4, since Euler inflated the cycles. Verdict: a regional density layer of this kind can run behind the budget for a few numbers per region per day and modulate group counts, the species mix inside the danger-eligible set and predator hunger (wider night search in lean phases); it creates no base visits by itself. Simulator: disagree with building the spatial offline runner first. Encounters depend on what it would have to copy (pathfinding, collision, canopy, chunk loading), while the real engine can already run headless and faster than real time with vanilla /tick sprint. Order: fix the budget defects; build an in-engine harness on seeded worlds with scripted bot players (a ServerPlayer on a fake connection, since NeoForge FakePlayers are not in the level and are neither sensed nor counted), the NaturalPopulations.enforce entry point and BehaviorLod test observers, logging the Codex metrics plus placement refusals by reason and tick time; then sweep the population layer offline, where it is pure math, using rates measured in the engine (encounters and kills per animal-hour at a given density); confirm the chosen settings in the engine. Build an agent-based offline copy only if engine sweeps prove too slow, calibrated against harness traces. Offline runs allow paired seeds; engine runs are not deterministic and need repetitions. Too hard to predict exact behaviour; good enough to rank designs once calibrated.
2026-10-01 (Claude Opus 5.5, wild births and performance discussion; not implemented): the user proposes male and female births limited by resources, from an initial density, instead of spawn rules, with the behaviour validated by birth, death and density statistics. Agree as the mechanism inside the simulated area: hunting and taming leave lasting consequences, regions differ by forage, juveniles add variety. Disagree that it replaces the population model. 1) Entities only tick within the simulation distance (12 chunks in the dev setup), so births, deaths and migration stop everywhere else and explored land keeps its initial density; the initial density, recolonization at the edge of the ticking area and a performance ceiling are spawn rules under other names. 2) Near a base the player is one more predator, and the measured small-population runs (predators lost in a median 8 days at 20 prey and 4 predators) predict local extinction where players live unless immigration refills it. 3) Behaviour sets stability here: predation only happens in full detail near players, at rates fixed by the code (a defensive herd with two healthy members within 32 blocks is almost unhuntable, prey must be at most 1.3 times the predator's width, hunting only at night, chases end after 15 s); birth, death and density statistics show that something is off but not which behaviour, different behaviours produce the same curves, and warnings and readability are not in them. 4) Cost: sexes, mating, nesting and young-guarding states, eggs or gestation, juveniles for about 40 species, and generations of a few in-game days to show within a session. ARK itself does not breed wild creatures; its spawn zones refill. Hybrid proposed: births and per-chunk forage stocks where entities tick; a regional ledger for unloaded land, calibrated by the in-game birth, death and density statistics; immigration from the ledger at the edge of the ticking area; the budget reduced to a performance ceiling. Performance (measure first with vanilla /jfr start and /perf start under /tick sprint in the harness): competing server load is vanilla farm animals (chunk generation seeds about 0.4 per chunk, about 90 within 128 blocks in grassland against 10 to 14 dinosaurs, and the budget deletes chunk-generated dinosaurs above 14 while the cows stay), fish, squid, dolphins, bats, axolotls and glow squid (per-player caps 20, 5, 15, 5, 5), and villages (villagers are the heaviest vanilla AI; their trades were themed, so a design call; drop the villages structure set). Gamerules: spawn_wandering_traders off, spawner_blocks_work off (mineshaft spawners), spread_vines off, spawn_monsters off unless spiders, the one vanilla hostile still spawning, are wanted; spawn_mobs off once births and an initial density replace spawning (it also stops chunk-generation spawns and the budget). Mod load, probably larger: every full-detail animal scans a 48 to 64-block box and casts up to 24 sight rays twice a second; vanilla collision and block-effect checks run over the whole body box every tick, also for dormant animals, and grow with volume (a Titanosaur box is 30 by 42 by 30 blocks), so skip physics for idle dormant animals on solid ground; pushing between large boxes; tracking at 12 chunks. Client, sharing the CPU in singleplayer: shaders run on the GPU and do not touch the server tick; Distant Horizons can keep LOD rendering with distant generation off (it generates Tectonic and Terralith terrain beyond view distance); GeckoLib animation cost grows with visible dinosaurs (entity culling, slower animation far away). Disabling buys entity budget, not a living world: going from 12 to 16 simulation chunks multiplies ticking chunks by 1.74, so only the ledger makes time pass where nobody is.
2026-10-01 (Claude Opus 5.5, measured): server tick time per entity on the GameTest server (flat grass floor, no players, afternoon, 16 animals per phase and 9 Titanosaurs, 200 warm-up and 400 measured ticks, timed around each entity tick with NeoForge EntityTickEvent; probe kept on branch claude/ai-cost-probe, not merged). Mean microseconds per entity per tick: cow 46; villager 134 without beds or jobs and 127 with a bed and a lectern each; Parasaur 67, Triceratops 116 and Tyrannosaurus 318 at full detail; Tyrannosaurus 283 in the ambient run (a few walked back into full detail) and 140 dormant; Titanosaur 7,966 at full detail (median 5,987, one tick of 1.1 s) and 3,287 dormant. A villager costs about three cows, and its cost is its brain (nine sensors with entity scans of 16 and 32 blocks, every stopped behaviour of the active activities retried every tick, job and bed searches over 48 blocks with paths to up to five candidates), paid by every villager within simulation distance since vanilla has no distance tiers. A dormant Tyrannosaurus already costs a villager and a dormant Titanosaur about 25, because collision, block-contact and fluid work grows with the body box and runs every tick whatever the tier; nine idle Titanosaurs take about 30 ms of the 50 ms tick. Correction to the earlier note: villages are not the main lever; the physics of large bodies and the full-detail AI of large species are. Next: skip physics for idle creatures on solid ground, a smaller terrain-collision box for giants, then re-measure with the probe.
2026-10-02 (Claude Opus 5.5, recorded sessions: summary and three tests to run): a way to measure the behaviour model in the real game instead of arguing from the source. Details: B07 (recorder), B08 and B09 (defects).
Done: the mod records every loaded creature of a play session (status twice a second, movement every tick near the player, every decision pass with the rule that chose the state, every sense check on the player, every path request and its outcome, stalls with the blocks around the body) into one file; Python turns it into a database, a ranked incident list and a replay page. A runner plays a session with nobody at the keyboard: a scripted player in the real client, the recording, then the analysis.
Run (from the repository root; JDK 25, Python with duckdb and plotly; a game window opens for about three minutes longer than the recording; not while another dev client runs): python Ark/tools/session_run.py [--world NAME | --new-world [--seed SEED]] [--time TICKS] [--seconds 300] [--delay 60] [--mode approach|stand]. --world copies that save and plays the copy (default: the save played last); --new-world has the client create a survival world. --time moves the clock forward to that time of day at the join; the recording starts about 1,300 ticks later with the default delay. approach walks to the nearest wild creature, stands within five blocks for 15 s, backs away and picks the next; stand does not move. The player starts healed and fed. For the run only: shaders off, windowed, muted; the user's options, shader setting and worlds are put back. Output in Ark/run/diagnostics/<session>/: the recording, session.duckdb, summary.json, incidents.jsonl, sight.json (what blocked each line of sight) and review.html; the console prints the summary. Exit code 2 means records are missing, 1 that nothing was recorded. To read one creature: python Ark/tools/session_analyze.py <session> --window ID FROM TO; any question: --sql "..." (tables decisions, decision_players, decision_nav, status_x, motion_x, events, entities, paths, terrain_blocks, ticks). AGENTS.md keeps runClient for the user; the user allowed this runner on 2026-10-02.
Observed in the first session (300 s, Raised Population, mountain forest, day time 6,640 to 12,640, 176 Ark creatures, mostly Pegomastax; complete, 215,858 records): 1) no creature ever heard the player: 17,337 sense checks, 5,996 while the player moved, none saw it move (the server overwrites a real player's previous position). 2) Within 32 blocks 3,486 of 3,839 checks had no line of sight (ground 2,303, trunks 977, leaves 206); within 16 blocks the player was noticed in 63 of 307 checks, 10 by sight and 53 by smell. A sleeping Carnotaurus did not notice a player standing 3.4 to 3.9 blocks from its body for ten seconds: its one sight ray clips a spruce trunk. 3) Trees block eyes, not bodies: 12 stalls of Ark creatures were collisions; 313 of the 434 times a creature held a path and did not move it was turning on the spot with the walk action (Pegomastax 18.5% of their path time). 4) The return-home loop is real (352 refused requests, 7 episodes), and 163 of 358 other refused paths were asked while the body was off the ground. 5) 25 Pegomastax looked for water for the whole session, two drank. Not covered: predators (those near the player were in their morning sleep, and after the player died and respawned none came within 82 blocks), chases, night, a fresh world. The scripted player is crude (stuck twice for 35 s, fell down slopes).
Schedule with the run config (night 13,000 to 23,000, carnivore day sleep 0.7, individual delay up to 600 ticks): carnivores sleep from 23,000 to about 8,800, roam until 13,000 and hunt at night; by day they consider a player only within 8 blocks of the body (funnel stage day_routine), and herbivores do the same at night.
Test 1, new world (morning; population and first decisions): python Ark/tools/session_run.py --new-world --seed ark-baseline --mode stand --seconds 300. Records day time about 1,300 to 7,300 around a player standing at the spawn point. Read: Ark creatures within 64 and 128 blocks at the start and the end and the time until the first one within 64 (status_x.player_gap); how they got there and left (entities.origin and note: budget_spawn against chunk generation; events leave with why and note); whether new bodies start badly (incidents path_refused_airborne with a small age_ticks, return_home_loop; decisions of bodies with origin spawn); tick time while chunks generate (ticks). Expect one budget group per five seconds up to 0.4 animals per chunk; B08 predicts loops among bodies whose first decision came in their first two ticks. Repeat with a second seed.
Test 2, afternoon (carnivores awake, quiet routine): python Ark/tools/session_run.py --world "Raised Population" --time 8000 --mode approach --seconds 180. Records about 9,300 to 12,900; the save starts beside a Carnotaurus, a Velociraptor and five Ravagers. Read: predator states (ROAM, not SLEEP, from about 9,400); the funnel per predator: day_routine beyond 8 blocks is the design, undetected inside 8 blocks is a miss, sensed should lead to a warning or an attack (incidents sensed_then_warning, attack, undetected_close, ignored_approach); herbivores flee or defend (fled_from_player); the sense table (heard should stay 0 until B09 is fixed) and sight.json.
Test 3, night (carnivores hunt with full senses, herbivores quiet): python Ark/tools/session_run.py --world "Raised Population" --time 12700 --mode approach --seconds 300. Read: how far away predators sense the player and by which sense; attack, pursuit, pursuit_blocked, chase_without_movement, strike_hit, strike_missed, gave_up, lost_sight; what follows a chase (return_home_loop, B08); damage and deaths of the player by source (events damage and death: vanilla spiders also attack at night, and a downed player lies still for about 55 s before dying and respawning at the world spawn); herbivores at stage day_routine.
For every run report: the integrity line, the day-time window (world), creatures and species near the player, the sense table, the funnel for predators and herbivores apart, the incident counts with the top five, the turn table, tick time. Bugs exposed and fixed: offline completion previously updated only Ark because the FTB call required an online player; it now grants by party/actor UUID. Inventory.add can transfer an item and return false on its final no-room iteration, suppressing NeoForge's pickup post event; a narrow ItemEntity mixin reports partial transfers as successful while preserving rejected/zero-transfer pickups. Argentavis continued its dive during the animated bite and passed the target before impact; it brakes during the pending strike, while the hit frame still rechecks reach and sight.
Remaining proposals: a whole-server process restart that reloads FTB quest files, dedicated-server spawn-protection checks, and client interactions/rendering. progression_restart is a disk-backed player/SavedData reload, not a process restart; fake-player registration and a payload-context test double support the real headless code paths.

Description: Tiers over creature levels: Common 1-20, Uncommon 21-40, Rare 41-60, Epic 61-80, Mythical 81-100, Primordial 100+. The tier is a label and a drop quality; stats stay on the level (LevelScaling). Creatures drop tiered parts, never finished gear: gear is crafted at the P14 benches, so recipe levels (F19) and the ages still decide what can be made, and the parts only decide its quality (output tier = the lowest tiered ingredient; only wild kills drop tiered parts). Quality scales durability (up to x3) more than stats (up to x1.5) and stays below the next material's Common (keratin armour 8 x1.5 = 12 < bronze 13); Rare and Epic get one capped affix, Mythical and Primordial two, from a small pool per item family; abilities stay on relics (F13). A tiered item works as Common until its holder reaches the tier's level (Ark's level-locked supply crates). Tooltips: the tier lives in a synced component arksurvivalreturns:quality, mirrored into minecraft:rarity (NeoForge-extensible enum: add Mythical, Primordial) and minecraft:tooltip_style (vanilla draws tooltip/<style>_frame and _background per stack; built like the Ark UI moss frame, animated by mcmeta). Obscure Tooltips: no 26.1 build (4.2.5 is 1.21.1, 5.0.0 is 1.21.11); its license forbids shipping a ported, patched or rebranded jar and reusing its code, so it can only ship unbranded from Modrinth once Obscuria releases 26.1, with an Ark style pack keyed on the rarities. Its nbt filter causes the detection failures: it compares the saved component patch with strict types (3 vs 3b), default components are absent, and unsynced components never reach the client. Apotheosis 26.1.2-9.0.3 exists but needs Apothic Enchanting and Spawners; only its idea is taken (rarity weights tied to an earned world tier).
Status: Under discussion (proposal 2026-09-30, Claude Opus 5.5). Decisions: 1) Mythical and Primordial sources: wild levels stop at 80 (Extreme 40-80) and clamp at 100, so proposed Mythical = rare alpha spawns in Severe/Extreme, Primordial = bosses and tames lifted past 100 by taming bonus levels (clamp raised); 2) skew the wild level roll toward the zone minimum (uniform makes half of Extreme Epic); 3) quality numbers, and steel's base at or above bronze Primordial (19.5); 4) the level each tier needs; 5) the affix pool; 6) which tier frames to draw.

Description: Record the actual first three minutes of an interactive Minecraft session, with player and creature coordinates, AI decisions, actions, navigation and collision evidence. Diagnose the reported daytime Carnotaurus eight-block reaction and apparent idle/non-pursuit. Related: P00 behaviour analysis and P21 population changes. Capture first, interpret the evidence afterwards.
Status:
Implemented; first real session recorded 2026-10-02 by an unattended client run (complete, 215,858 records). A session played by the user is still pending. Codex's plan of 2026-10-01 follows; the implementation notes are at the end.
Observed source: WildlifeGoal.routineAllows gates ordinary daytime carnivore player candidates by WildlifeSenses.bodyDistance <= Config.WAKE_DISTANCE (default 8 blocks between collision boxes); intruding uses < 8. Full land decisions run every 10 simulation ticks. Creative/spectator and Peaceful filtering, sensory competition (nearest 24 eligible candidates), awareness/warning timers, choreography holds, turn-in-place steering and navigation can separately explain inactivity. WildlifeMind.reason already exposes the winning rule. LandWildlife.allowPath shares eight path requests per level/tick; deferral returns without a path failure, so failedPaths alone cannot diagnose it. These are code facts and candidate explanations, not a diagnosis of the user's unrecorded encounter.
Capture contract: a one-shot arm for the next world join, disabled normally. A small client-ready signal starts the clock when the player can control the world, excluding loading screens. Record 180 seconds of unpaused real time; stop on the first server tick at/after the deadline or earlier on player disconnect/world shutdown/manual stop. Respawn does not restart the timer; dimension changes are events. Include monotonic elapsed time, active elapsed time, server tick and per-dimension game/day clock; record pauses and lag rather than equating three minutes to 3600 ticks. Show start/completion and the saved path; reaching the deadline leaves the game open. Optional marker command/key adds a timestamped incident while playing.
Scope and cadence: enumerate every already-loaded living mob in server levels, including Ark land, aquatic, flying and tamed creatures plus vanilla animals/prey with basic fields. Record actual loaded/ticking eligibility and last-ticked/last-decision timestamps. Unloaded entities are unavailable; never force chunks or infer their unseen movement. Baseline snapshots every 10 ticks (2 Hz at 20 TPS); player and creatures within 64 blocks of the player's body, plus active interaction/target participants, get lightweight position/rotation/motion/collision samples each simulation tick. Exact-tick hooks capture Ark decision passes, state/action/target changes, path attempts, strikes and lifecycle events regardless of snapshot cadence. Keep a few seconds of close-range history after disengagement. Ticking at less than 20 TPS reduces the real-time sample rate and is visible in timestamps. Vanilla gets generic status/navigation/lifecycle only; do not label its uninstrumented decisions with invented Ark reasons.
Session header and identity: versioned schema, session ID, build/commit and dirty/build fingerprint, effective mod and AI/population config, world seed/dimension and relevant gamerules, difficulty, actual render and simulation distances, shader/Distant Horizons settings when available. Use a small session entity ID mapped once to UUID/species/type/group/initial dimensions; record bounding-box size changes. Record player position/eye position, look, health, mode, sprint/crouch, movement and relevant gear/sense modifiers, attacks, damage and block interactions. Preserve timestamps and original numeric precision in raw evidence.
Creature schema: position, velocity, body/head yaw, collision bounds, health, tame/rider/torpor/no-AI flags, behaviour tier, behaviour state, action, active goal/controller, selected focus/target, last-known stimulus and home. Ark decisions include observation inputs, winning reason, hunger/thirst/fatigue/awareness, memory/warning/chase/recovery timers, day/night/sleep schedule and choreography hold/phase. Cache the actual sensory result and source (sight, hearing, scent, noise or alarm), range/LOS/FOV checks actually evaluated and candidate eligibility/rejection (day routine, mode, Peaceful, disguise, cap, competing target). A skipped check is not-evaluated, never false. Preserve bounded candidate summaries and the participating player's rejection/score so a missing target is explainable.
Movement and combat evidence: intended destination/speed, move-control operation, turn angle/pivot hold, existing path identity/node progress/reachable/done/stuck status, request outcome (success, failed, reused, budget-deferred, unloaded terrain, no ground), failed-path count and chase abandonment. Copy path nodes only when a path changes. Capture attack request, cooldown/windup, hit-frame resolution, range/LOS/torpor rejection and actual damage. Record overlapping/touching body boxes and measured displacement, keeping collision evidence distinct from a rendered model silhouette. On sustained attempted movement without progress or repeated path failure, take a bounded, deduplicated snapshot of loaded block states/collision shapes around the body and next path node, including supporting ground and capture bounds/truncation. This supports the tree hypothesis; coordinates alone cannot identify an obstruction. Sample rendered/controller state for the looked-at nearby Ark creature in the client module when practical, matched by UUID/server tick; server action cues alone do not prove what was drawn.
Observation must not change the experiment: copy immutable primitive data on the owning game thread and serialize/write on a single bounded background queue. Instrument branches/results already executed; never rerun think(), senses, pathfinding, random draws, or mutating/lazy mind/home/attachment getters just to log. Avoid bulk reuse of DinoDebugSnapshot.capture: it reflects fields and serializes full saved entity data for one spyglass target and is too broad for continuous population recording. Use explicit read-only accessors and realm adapters instead. Record spawn/load, unload, death, despawn, budget cull and dimension transitions separately; initial presence is not a fresh spawn. Add entity counts, tick timings, recorder capture cost, queue depth and written/dropped record counts. Queue overflow or writer failure must visibly mark the capture incomplete, with sequence gaps and time ranges; never silently call a truncated trace complete. Measure overhead before choosing final cadence; a target of <1 ms average capture work per tick is a goal, not a measured guarantee.
Storage: one append-only UTF-8 session.jsonl under Ark/run/diagnostics/<session-id>/, already ignored by Ark/.gitignore. Typed header/entity/snapshot/motion/decision/event/terrain/health/footer records carry sequence and tick IDs. Flush about once per second off-thread; graceful end drains and closes with stop reason and integrity counts. Abrupt termination retains complete written lines; analyzer discards a partial final line and reports missing footer/gaps. This is best-effort crash recovery, not power-loss durability. Compress to .jsonl.gz after successful close, retaining the raw file until the archive is verified. Store repeated constants once; emit large path/terrain records only on change. For scale, 100 mobs at 2 Hz for 180 s is 36000 baseline rows before close-range motion/events; file size and overhead must be measured.
Python analysis: stdlib json/gzip/pathlib/argparse for streaming, validation and interrupted-tail recovery; DuckDB as the single query/storage dependency for typed tables, interval queries and optional Parquet export; Plotly for an offline HTML review with a time slider, top-down tracks, entity selection, state/action timeline, distance-to-player/awareness plots and short incident windows. Use explicit schemas and source sequence references, not mixed-event JSON schema guessing. Scripts belong in Ark/tools/. Initial analyzer outputs summary.json, incidents.jsonl and a local session.duckdb; visualization derives review.html. Token efficiency comes from Python computing counts, coverage, durations and ranked incident episodes first: read a compact summary and request only the few seconds around a creature/event. Preserve raw evidence for every loaded creature; do not paste the full log into the conversation. Position playback reconstructs observations, not an exact executable world simulation, and interpolation/unknown intervals must be labelled. This task does not need a separate agent-based simulator or a live Python process attached to the JVM.
Analysis after the playtest: classify ignored approach versus sensed-but-warning/holding, target acquired without progress, deferred/failed path, body collision, lost visibility, abandoned chase, unsuccessful strike, cosmetic idle mismatch and actual successful responses. Report normal reference episodes as well as anomalies, with entity ID, start/end tick, distances and source events; suspicious intervals are hypotheses until their trace is checked. Large tier/sample gaps and missing obstacle evidence remain explicit unknowns.
Test sequence for the user: shaders off, render distance 10, record the actual simulation distance separately; use Survival for an ordinary aggression test and record difficulty. Start with natural daylight behaviour: approach from beyond 12 blocks through 10/8/6, pause for warning time, touch the collision bounds if possible, retreat and circle any tree. A short open-ground comparison with the same individual is useful if feasible. Free interaction remains valid; no forced night/teleports/spawns or balance fixes before the baseline. Current Ark/config/dev-runtime.properties specifies renderDistance=24 and simulationDistance=12 and prepareDevRuntime can reapply them; implementation needs a deliberate recording-profile override so the intended 10-chunk setting survives launch. The user launches and plays; the recorder automatically saves at timeout or early exit.
Implementation order: add one-shot lifecycle and writer; add typed snapshots plus decision/navigation/combat/terrain hooks for the relevant controllers; implement integrity checks and compact Python analysis; verify recording; let the user play; then inspect the saved session and make the replay useful for actual incidents. Validate timeout/pause/early-close/truncated-tail/queue-overflow, ID reuse and unload/reload, all realm coverage, no extra loaded chunks and no state/RNG changes from observation. Controlled fixtures should distinguish daytime filtering, Creative/Peaceful exclusions, warning holds, a blocked route, budget deferral and a successful chase. Follow workspace checks for gameplay-adjacent Java changes: Gradle wrapper build and runGameTestServer; runData if adding generated test instances. Plan-only task did not require these builds. No runClient is launched by the agent.
Library references checked 2026-10-01: https://docs.python.org/3/library/json.html ; https://docs.python.org/3/library/gzip.html ; https://duckdb.org/docs/current/data/json/loading_json ; https://duckdb.org/docs/current/clients/python/data_ingestion ; https://plotly.com/python/interactive-html-export/ ; https://plotly.com/python/animations/ .

Item: Land AI: return-home loop, airborne first decision, chase that stops short
Description: Three defects of the land routine, seen in B07 recordings of a scripted Carnotaurus encounter on open flat grass. 1) Return-home loop: at its home block the animal asks for a path to where it already stands; the request returns false, six such decision passes call abandonChase, and abandonChase re-arms the 200-tick recovery, so RETURN_HOME never ends. In WildlifeMind.step RETURN_HOME outranks awareness: the animal senses the player (awareness 1, warning timer counting) and stands still; only the escape and night-herd rules get through, and a hit is not answered. 2) Airborne first decision: a new body is not on the ground during its first two ticks (the first move is zero, gravity lands it on the second), and vanilla ground navigation refuses every path of a body that is neither on the ground nor in liquid. A decision pass in that window (2 of the 10 phases, creatures not loaded from disk) fails six roam requests at once, gives up and enters loop 1 at its spawn point for good. 3) Chase stops short: a wide body consumes its path nodes within half its width, so the path runs out with the body still blocks away from the target and outside melee reach; every new request equals the finished path and returns false, six failures abandon the chase, and loop 1 follows once the animal is home.
Status:
Open: found 2026-10-01 by the B07 fixture, not fixed (the B07 playtest is recorded first, so the baseline stays as it is). Candidates until that session confirms them in real play. Evidence: python Ark/tools/session_analyze.py Ark/run/diagnostics/gametest reports chase_without_movement and pursuit_blocked (no_path with the body one to two and a half blocks from the player, the path ran out, nothing in the terrain capture); two runs whose first decision came in the animal's first two ticks reported path_refused_airborne and return_home_loop (0 blocks from home, the player sensed on 21 passes at 4.9 blocks, still in it when the recording ended).
Fix candidates: in WildlifeGoal.move treat a request that is already satisfied as arrival, not as a failed path, and end RETURN_HOME on arrival; skip decision passes until the body is on the ground or in water; chase by the gap between the bodies until melee reach, not to the path's end; let a hit and a sensed intruder override RETURN_HOME.
2026-10-02, first real session (B07): 1) seen in real play: 352 return-home path requests refused (6 Pegomastax, 1 Parasaur), 7 loop episodes, e.g. Pegomastax #206 standing on its home block for 58 s (117 passes, 19 give-ups). 2) is wider than a new body: 163 of the 358 other refused requests were made on a decision pass that found the body off the ground (stepping down a slope, hopping), at any age (roam 96 of 101, flee 22 of 22, investigate 20 of 24). 3) was not exercised: every carnivore slept (daytime).

Item: Creature senses and movement: findings of the first real session
Description: Found by the first real session of B07 (Ark/run/diagnostics/20261002-060701-4c26: mountain forest, daytime, 176 Ark creatures, mostly Pegomastax). 1) Hearing never works on a real player. WildlifeSenses.detect decides that the target moves by comparing its position with xo/yo/zo, and the server sets a real player's previous position to the new one on every movement packet (ServerGamePacketListenerImpl.handleMovePlayer, absSnapTo), so the difference is always zero: 17,337 sense checks on the player, 5,996 of them while the player moved, flagged as moving 0, heard 0. The GameTest player is moved by setPos, which leaves xo behind, so the tests pass. 2) Sight is one ray from eye centre to eye centre and is blocked most of the time: within 32 blocks 3,486 of 3,839 checks had no line of sight; first block on the ray: ground 2,303, trunk 977, leaves 206 (tools/session_sight.py, which agrees with the game on all 3,839). Small animals have their eyes half a block above sloping ground. A sleeping Carnotaurus (3.6 wide, 6 tall) had the player 3.4 to 3.9 blocks from its body for ten seconds and saw nothing: its ray clips the corner of a spruce trunk by 7 mm. Within 16 blocks the player was noticed in 63 of 307 checks: 10 by sight, 53 by smell (downwind only), none by hearing. 3) Turning on the spot. With a path and the WALK action, bodies stand and rotate at 1.5 to 4 degrees a tick: 1,263 turns by 51 Pegomastax, 364 of them a second or longer (longest 3 s), 18.5% of their path time (Parasaur 31%, Triceratops 23%). 313 of the 434 no-progress stalls of Ark creatures are this; none of the 434 is a collision, and collisions with blocks account for 12 Ark stalls in all, so trees block sight far more than they block bodies. 4) Thirst: 25 Pegomastax spent 4,654 decision passes in SEEK_WATER, which moves like roaming; two drank. 5) Fleeing: 152 flee requests by 25 Pegomastax found no destination; two Parasaur had 120 flee paths refused and were cornered 19 times.
Status: Open: found 2026-10-02, not fixed. One five-minute session with a scripted player, so the counts are a first measure, not a distribution. Fix candidates: 1) take the player's movement from ServerPlayer.getKnownMovement (or a position the mod keeps from the previous tick) instead of xo; give the GameTest a player that moves the way a client does. 2) several rays (to the target's head, chest and feet; from the front of a wide body) or sight that ignores one thin trunk for bodies wider than it; decide whether leaves hide a player. 3) a faster turn or walking the arc instead of standing; do not show WALK while turning. 4) a water search for SEEK_WATER. Re-measure each with python Ark/tools/session_run.py and compare the sense and turn tables the analyzer prints.
